title: Job Search, Offers, and Career
description:
Job search, offers and career: application materials, search strategy and negotiation.

---

Everything in Phases 1–14 is evidence. This phase packages that evidence, distributes it through
a measurable funnel, and converts output into a decision you can defend four years from now.

Three structural facts frame the phase:
1. **Search is a conversion problem, not a talent problem.** Distribution strategy beats average
   ability; throughput and conversion rate are both learnable.
2. **The recruiter screen is the highest-leverage conversation in the search** and the one most
   people prepare worst — the only stage where you hold more information about the employer's
   constraints than they hold about your flexibility.
3. **The offer you accept is a bundle, not a salary.** Base, bonus, equity, vesting, dilution,
   benefits, leave, manager, learning curve, and reversibility differ by more than headline numbers.

**How to use this phase.** 15.1 builds material, 15.2 runs the funnel, 15.3 converts output into a
deliberate choice. Read 15.3 before 15.2 — knowing what a good outcome looks like changes how you
source, screen, and negotiate.

**Non-negotiable discipline:** never fabricate a metric, scale, customer count, or revenue figure.
Interviewers probe numbers, and a number you cannot defend in two follow-up sentences is worse than
no number. Everything below is about making *true* numbers legible. Likewise, describe method and
structure rather than fabricating survey statistics or company salaries.

## Outreach Message Templates

**Positioning statement (write once, use everywhere).**
`I am a <role> who specializes in <problem A> and <problem B>. Most recently I <one outcome>.`

### Referral request
```
Subject: Referral for <role> at <company>?
Hi <name> — <one specific line of context: last interaction, shared project, or something of
theirs I read>.
I'm looking for <target role> roles in <market>. I'm at <company> doing <domain> work, most
recently <headline outcome>.
I saw the <role> posting / heard you're close to that team. Would you be comfortable referring
me? Happy to write the blurb — if you're too far from that team, no problem at all.
Positioning in one line: <positioning statement>
Resume: <link>   One relevant project: <link>
Thanks either way — <name>.
```

### Cold outreach to a hiring manager
```
Subject: <specific thing> — <your role>
Hi <name> — I saw <specific recent work: launch, post, talk, open-source release>.
I'm a <role> working on <domain>. The reason I'm writing: <one specific overlap between their
stated problem and something you have actually done, with a result>. Most relevantly, <one
project in one sentence, with a link>.
I'm not asking you to sponsor a job process. If it's useful I'd be glad to share what I found
in <the domain>; if you're hiring or know someone who is, I'd welcome an introduction.
```

### Cold outreach to a recruiter
```
Subject: <role> — <domain> — <years> years
Hi <name> — <role> with <N> years in <domain>, currently at <company>. Most recent:
<headline outcome with a number or concrete scope>.
Two things that may be relevant to roles you place: <one quantified capability> and <one
adjacent capability>. I'm looking for <target role> in <market>, <remote/hybrid/onsite>,
available after <date>.
Where I'm a fit: <one line tying your stack to a common requirement>. Resume: <link>
```

### Follow-up after an interview
```
Subject: Thank you — <role> at <company>
Hi <name> — thanks for the conversation about <specific thing: system, problem, decision>.
<One new piece of value: a clarification I under-explained, a link, a thought I had after.>
I'm very interested in the <specific> scope. Happy to provide anything else that would help.
```

### Post-rejection follow-up
```
Subject: After <company> — <role>
Hi <name> — thanks for the time and for the honest feedback. <One specific thing you will do
differently.>
I'd love to be considered for <future scope or team> when timing lines up. And if anyone else
on your side is hiring <skill>, I'd welcome an introduction.
```

### Networking / informational interview
```
Subject: 30 minutes on <team> at <company>
Hi <name> — <context line>. I'm <role> working on <domain>.
I'm not looking for a job right now / I'm exploring <adjacent area> and I'd value 30 minutes
on what <team> actually works on day to day. Happy to send a few questions in advance.
```
Always end an informational interview with: "Is there anyone you think I should talk to about
<adjacent team>?" — that question is what converts it into referrals.

### Cold outreach to an editor
```
Subject: Pitch — <specific, evidence-backed claim about X>
Hi <name> — I want to write about <X>, and the angle is that <the specific claim most write-ups
get wrong>. Supporting material: <a project, a benchmark with methodology, a migration I ran>.
Draft outline: <three bullets>. Previously published at <link>. Not pitching anything else —
happy to time it to a slot that suits you.
```

## Tracker Schema

Two tabs: `Pipeline` (one row per application) and `Metrics` (formulas).

**Pipeline columns.**

| Column | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| id | text | `COMPANY-role-YYYYMMDD` |
| company / role_title / level_scope | text | your read of the level |
| req_id_url / jd_url | text, link | re-apply, prepping |
| date_applied | date | velocity, timing |
| source | enum | referral / recruiter / board / cold / alumni / inbound |
| referrer / contact | text | direct lines beat portals |
| resume_variant | enum | backend-systems / data-ml / frontend-product / general |
| fit_score | 1–5 | set *before* applying |
| stage | enum | applied / screen / technical / onsite / offer / rejected / ghosted / withdrawn |
| stage_date_last | date | drives follow-up queue |
| days_in_stage | formula | `=TODAY()-stage_date_last` |
| next_action / due_date | text, date | **drives the daily work view** |
| followup_count | 0–3 | prevents over-following |
| rejection_stage / rejection_reason | enum, text | the diagnostic pair |
| market_note | text | band heard, level heard, team signals |
| screen_notes / tech_notes / onsite_notes | text | per-dimension scores 1–5 |
| salary_researched | text | low–high, with source and date |
| offer_base / offer_bonus_pct / offer_signon | number | |
| offer_equity_units / offer_equity_type | number, enum | RSU / option / none |
| offer_notes | text | clawback, start date, contingencies |
| reapply_date / archive | date, bool | filter closed rows out yearly |

**Metrics formulas.**
```
applications_this_week = COUNTIFS(stage_date_last, ">=" & this_monday)
screen_rate           = COUNTIFS(stage, "<>applied") / COUNTIFS(stage, "<>Withdrawn")
screens_by_source     = COUNTIFS(source, "referral", stage, "<>applied")
screen_rate_by_source = screens_by_source / COUNTIF(source, "referral")
offers_by_source      = COUNTIFS(source, "referral", stage, "offer")
median_cycle_days     = MEDIAN(days from applied to first stage advance)
```
Report weekly on one screen: applications, screens, onsites, offers, stage conversion, source mix,
fit-score calibration. Then pick the weakest transition and choose one experiment for the coming week.

**Dashboard rules.** Sort by `due_date` for the daily view, `stage` for the pipeline view. Flag
anything with `days_in_stage` past your own threshold — that is your follow-up queue. Flag `fit_score`
5 rows that have gone stale; those are your highest-value follow-ups.

## Negotiation Script Set

```
1. OPENING (recruiter call)      "Before specifics — how is the role scoped and leveled, and how is
                                  comp structured for that level? I want to compare the right things."
2. LEVEL ASK                     "Given the scope — owning X end to end with Y and Z as partners — my
                                  experience lines up with <L+1>. How does leveling work, and who would
                                  I need to convince? Here's the work that supports it: <2 examples>."
3. BAND DISCOVERY                "What does the approved range look like for this level, and where does
                                  my experience sit inside it? I'd rather optimize for the whole
                                  package than negotiate one line item."
4. RANGE ANSWER                  "For total cash I'm targeting the upper part of the band for this scope —
                                  call it <low>–<high>. For base specifically I'm at <number> and I
                                  have real flexibility on structure."
5. COMPETING OFFER (truth only)  "I have a written offer at <level> with <structure>, decision by
                                  <real date>. The scope here is what I care most about; the package is
                                  close to comparable. If you can move on the items below, I'd have
                                  difficulty declining."
6. THE PACKAGE ASK               "1. Base at <number>. 2. Initial grant of <N> shares sized to the level.
                                  3. Signing bonus of <amount> covering what I forfeit leaving now.
                                  4. Off-cycle comp review at <month> tied to scope.
                                  If base is fixed, I'm happy to move any of 2–4 instead."
7. SIGNING BONUS CASE            "The number is the one-time forfeiture: <pro-rated bonus> plus
                                  <unvested equity>, net of tax. An equivalent one-time equity grant
                                  works for me. Can you check with <approver>? I'll put it in writing."
8. TRADE                         "Base is fixed — understood. Would the company be open to <sign-on /
                                  one-time equity top-up / off-cycle refresh>? I'm flexible on <X>."
9. CLOSE                         "Based on <summarize package>, I'm in. Confirm in writing: base, bonus
                                  target, <N> <RSUs/options> vesting <schedule>, strike <price>,
                                  sign-on <amount> with <clawback>, title <X>, start <date>."
10. EXTEND A DEADLINE            "I have a decision point on <date> I need to honor. I'm close here. Can
                                  I have until <date>? I can give you my answer in writing within hours
                                  of that date so your team can use the time."
11. RECRUITER ADVOCATE REQUEST   "Would you take this to <HM/comp> for me? Here's the case in one
                                  paragraph: <scope>, <market evidence with dates>, <my results>,
                                  <the ask>, <my flexibility>. Forward it as-is if you like."
12. HM SCOPE CONVERSATION        "Two things about the role, not the money: where the scope lands on
                                  level, and where you expect this hire in twelve months. If the scope
                                  is what I described, what would it take to make the package match?"
13. DEGRADING GRACEFULLY         "I hear you — the band is where it is. Straightforward: that puts me
                                  below market for this scope, which is why I can't say yes today. Can
                                  you check one alternative — <specific>? If not, I respect it and I'll
                                  tell the other company I'm going with them."
14. DECLINING                    "I've decided to go with <company>. I wanted you to hear it from me
                                  first. Thanks for <specific thing>. If you need a <skill> person, call me."
```

## Offer Comparison Spreadsheet Layout

**Tabs:** `Inputs` · `Normalize` · `Benefits` · `Scenarios` · `3-Year` · `Decision`.

**Tab 1 — Inputs** (raw, as received; do not analyze here): company, level/scope, location/work model,
start date, base, target bonus %, equity type, equity units, strike, vesting schedule, cliff, sign-on
(+ clawback), other cash, refresh policy, treatment of unvested on termination, written deadline.

**Tab 2 — Normalize** (one row per offer; formula in the cell comment).

| Line | Formula | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Base | input | | | |
| Bonus (yr 1) | `base × bonus% × (months/12)` | | | |
| Bonus (steady) | `base × bonus% × realism(0.8–1.0)` | | | |
| Sign-on + other cash (yr 1) | `input × (1 − t_one_time)` | | | |
| **Year-1 cash, net** | sum | | | |
| COL index to your city | `=index(you)/index(city)` | | | |
| **Base, COL-adjusted** | `base × COL index` | | | |
| Share price used | input + date | | | |
| RSU value/unit | `=share price` | | | |
| Option value/unit | `=MAX(0, price − strike) × p(in-the-money)` | | | |
| Gross equity at full vest | `units × value/unit` | | | |
| Vesting factor yr 1 | `=0.25` (4 yr monthly, mid-year start ≈0.19) | | | |
| Tax at vest | `× (1 − t_vest)` | | | |
| Liquidity / time discount | mature RSU 0.85; startup 0.3–0.5 | | | |
| P(outcome) | startup: your estimate | 1.0 | 1.0 | |
| **PV equity (2–3 yr)** | product of the above | | | |
| **Year-1 total, normalized** | cash + PV equity + benefits | | | |
| **3-year total** | roll forward w/ refresh + 1 promo | | | |

**Tab 3 — Benefits** — annual dollars, only what you will use: employer health contribution for *your*
plan and family status; retirement match as % of salary; paid leave (days × (base+bonus)/working days);
public holidays; parental leave (weeks × rate); equipment/remote budget; learning budget; on-call
compensation; relocation after tax if you will stay past the minimum; legal fee benefit. **Total row.**

**Tab 4 — Scenarios** — the sensitivity that matters: share price at −30%, base, +30%, and +100% only
if credible; multiply through equity PV and the 3-year total for each offer.

**Tab 5 — 3-Year** — per offer: Year / base (with one promotion) / refresh units / equity value /
benefits / total / cumulative. Then repeat for share price −30% and for "I leave at month 18" (only
vested equity counts).

**Tab 6 — Decision** — filled in *before* you negotiate:
```
Expected 3-year total (normalized):        $___
Confidence range:                            $___ – $___
Non-monetary factor I will trade money for: <scope | manager | mission | stability | growth>
Chosen offer and why (one paragraph):        ___
```

**Use in this order:** Inputs → Normalize → Benefits → Scenarios → 3-Year → Decision. Writing the
Decision tab first stops you negotiating toward a number instead of toward the outcome you chose.

All figures are illustrative constructions, not real offers from real companies. They show the
arithmetic. Substitute your own numbers, and never cite these as market data.

Shared assumptions: combined tax + vesting withholding `t = 30%`; one-time payments taxed at 35%;
bonus realism factor `0.9`; liquidity/time discount on mature public RSUs `0.85`; refresh = 25% of
the initial grant, 4-year monthly vest; 250 working days per year.

## Example 1 — RSU-heavy vs cash-and-title-heavy (mature vs late-stage private)

**Candidate.** Staff-level backend engineer, 9 years, one time zone shift.

| | **Offer A** (large public, hybrid) | **Offer B** (late-stage private, remote) |
|---|---|---|
| Title / level | Staff / L5 | Senior Staff (director-level, no people mgmt) |
| Base | 240,000 | 275,000 |
| Target bonus | 15% | 10% |
| Equity | 22,000 RSUs @ $58 | 30,000 options, strike $2.10 |
| Sign-on / other | 20,000 | 35,000 + 10,000 relocation |
| Health | 18,000 (family) | 9,000 (employee only) |
| Match | 50% of first 6% = 3% | 4%, 3-year cliff |
| PTO | 20 days + 9 holidays | "unflexible" (price at ~12 used days) |

**Step 1 — year-1 cash.** A: `240,000 + 240,000×0.15 + 20,000×0.65 = 289,000`.
B: `275,000 + 275,000×0.10 + 45,000×0.65 = 331,750`. Raw cash favors B by 42,750.

**Step 2 — cost of living.** New-city COL index 118 vs current 100.
`A base, COL-adjusted = 240,000 × 118/100 = 283,200` vs `B = 275,000`. **The ordering flips** —
A was never lower; it was a higher-COL city with a lower nominal base.

**Step 3 — equity (the decisive step).**
```
A (RSU):  value/unit = 58.00;  yr-1 vested 22,000×0.25 = 5,500 sh
          5,500 × 58 = 319,000 × (1−0.30) = 223,300 × 0.85 = 189,805  ≈ 189,800
B (option): intrinsic = max(0, 2.10 − 2.10) = 0.00
          The grant is exactly at the money. 30,000 units is NOT 30,000 shares of value.
          Illustrative long-dated option approximation:
          0.40 P(in the money) × 0.60 spread × (1−0.30) = 0.168 per option
          yr-1 vested 7,500 × 0.168 = 1,260 × 0.50 (private illiquidity) ≈ 630
```
A's equity is worth ~**$189,800** for the year; B's ~**$630**. This is the entire decision.
**Insight:** never compare unit counts across offer types; never normalize an option count against an
RSU count.

**Step 4 — benefits, annualized.**
```
A: health 18,000 + match 240,000×0.03 = 7,200 + PTO 20 × (276,000/250 = 1,104) = 22,080
   + holidays 9 × 1,104 = 9,936                                    → 57,216
B: health 9,000 + own plan ~9,000 = 18,000 + match 0 in yr 1 (3-yr cliff)
   + 12 × (302,500/250 = 1,210) = 14,520                          → 32,520
```

**Step 5 — year-1 totals.**

| Line | A | B |
|---|---|---|
| Cash | 289,000 | 331,750 |
| Equity (net, discounted) | 189,800 | 630 |
| Benefits | 57,200 | 32,500 |
| **Year-1 total** | **536,000** | **365,000** |

**Step 6 — three-year view (with A promoted at month 18).**
```
A: Yr1 523,000 | Yr2 262,000 base + 39,300 bonus + 189,800 equity + 62,600 benefits = 571,700
   Yr3 265,500 + 31,860 + 189,800 + 62,600 = 553,760   → 3-yr ≈ 1,648,400
   at share price −30% ($40.60): equity/yr = 5,500×40.60×0.595 = 132,838 → ≈ 1,504,900
B: cash (302,500×2.5) + 29,250 = 835,500; benefits 32,500×2.5 = 81,250 → ≈ 916,750
   Upside case (3× last round, 4M preferred at 1× $2.10 = 8.4M preference, 15M FD post-money):
     exit 60M − 8.4M = 51.6M / 15M = 3.44/sh → intrinsic 1.34 × 30,000 = 40,200
     × 0.70 tax × 0.50 illiquidity = 14,070 → 3-yr ≈ 930,820
```
**Verdict.** Even in B's upside case it is roughly 700,000 worse over three years. The right
negotiation for B is not about base; it is a meaningful signing bonus, an above-market refresh in
writing, and confirmation of the strike and share count. **Lesson:** the first question to ask about
any option grant is the strike and the current share price.

## Example 2 — Startup equity, probability-weighted

**Candidate.** Senior engineer, 7 years, data/infra, currently at a mid-size public company.

| | **Offer S** (seed/Series A) | **Offer P** (stable private) |
|---|---|---|
| Base | 205,000 (below market) | 228,000 |
| Bonus | None | 10% |
| Equity | 180,000 options, strike $1.40 | 9,000 RSUs |
| Sign-on | 10,000 | 15,000 |
| Refresh | None stated — ask | Not stated |

**Dilution analysis.**
```
FD shares now              = 12,000,000   your 180,000 = 1.50%
Pool authorized 2,000,000; granted 900,000; unallocated 1,100,000
Next primary round         =  3,000,000
future FD = 12,000,000 + 1,100,000 + 3,000,000 = 16,100,000
your future %              = 180,000 / 16,100,000 = 1.12%
relative dilution          = (1.50 − 1.12)/1.50 = 25%
```
**You lose a quarter of your ownership to hiring and the next round, independent of performance.**

**Scenario analysis.** Assumptions stated so they can be challenged: downside 60% (no liquidity event),
base 25% (2× current price, year four), upside 15% (6×, year five). Preferred: 7,000,000 shares, 1×
non-participating, $1.40.

```
Downside:  $0

Base (exit = 2 × 1.40 × 12,000,000 = 33.6M):
  preference 7,000,000 × 1.40 = 9,800,000
  remaining  = 23,800,000 / 16,100,000 FD = 1.478/sh
  intrinsic  = max(0, 1.478 − 1.40) = 0.078
  gross 180,000 × 0.078 = 14,040 × 0.70 tax = 9,828 × 0.50 illiquidity = 4,914

Upside (exit = 100.8M):
  remaining = 100.8M − 9.8M = 91.0M / 16.1M = 5.652/sh → intrinsic 4.252
  gross 180,000 × 4.252 = 765,360 × 0.70 = 535,752 × 0.50 = 267,876

EV = 0.60×0 + 0.25×4,914 + 0.15×267,876 = 0 + 1,228 + 40,181 = $41,410
```
**Expected value of the "180,000 options" ≈ $41,000** — not $250,000, and not "180,000 units."

**Comparison.**
```
S yr-1 cash = 205,000 + 10,000×0.65 = 211,500
P yr-1 cash = 228,000 + 22,800 + 15,000×0.65 = 260,550
P's cash advantage in yr 1 = 49,050; over 3 yrs (ignoring raises) ≈ 122,600
P's equity is RSU-based, so it actually delivers: 9,000 × ~1.00 (P's private share value)
S's expected equity = 41,410 in expectation, 60% of the time zero.
```
**P beats S by roughly 80,000–120,000 in expected value over three years, before counting that P's
equity is a promise rather than an option.**

**Correct negotiation for S** — leverage is in cash, not shares:
```
1. Base to 225,000 (they almost certainly have room; this is the biggest lever)
2. Signing bonus 30,000 to bridge the base gap and forfeited bonus
3. Evergreen refresh clause (strike re-set every 12 months) — the single most valuable long-dated
   option term, and many companies will agree to it
4. Written refresh policy by level, since none is stated
5. Confirm the 409A refresh schedule — a low 409A lowers your exercise tax basis now
```
If they move 20,000 of base, accept and take the option as free upside. Do not trade a below-market
base for a large unit count.

## Example 3 — Level negotiation: a mid-level offer re-leveled upward

**Situation.** 7 years of experience; recruiter opens at L4 / mid-level. This compounds for years.

**Step 1 — get the scope in writing.**
```
Asked:   "What does this role own in its first year?"
Answer:  "You'll own <service> end to end, plus design for <adjacent area>, with two engineers as
          partners, and you'll be a reviewer on <larger area>."
```
End-to-end service ownership plus design authority over an area plus review authority across a larger
area is L5 work at most companies, regardless of title.

**Step 2 — the framing.** Note what this does: it never says "I deserve more money." It disputes the
*level of the job*, which is set by a calibration process driven by the hiring manager, not the
recruiter.
> "I'm going to be direct: I'm being offered L4, and I want to flag that the scope described is L5 work
> at the companies I know. Concretely: end-to-end ownership including <X>, design authority over <Y>,
> and review responsibility across <Z> — plus the background I mentioned, where I did <the equivalent>
> at <current company>. I'm not asking to skip a level. I'm asking whether this role is leveled
> correctly. If it can move to L5, I want to work there. If the company genuinely wants L4 scope, I
> want to know now so we're both clear."

**Step 3 — the response branches.**
- *Manager agrees and re-levels:* the whole package re-bases. Illustrative, where each level is ~15–20%
  on base and ~1.7× on the initial grant at $58/share:
  ```
  L4: base 195,000 | grant  9,000 × 58 = 522,000 | 10% bonus
  L5: base 225,000 | grant 15,000 × 58 = 870,000 | 15% bonus
  yr-1 delta = 30,000 base + 6,750 bonus + (6,000 × 58 × 0.70 × 0.85 = 207,096) = 243,846
  3-yr delta > 700,000, because refreshes are sized off level too.
  ```
- *Manager says the scope is L4:* then the scope needs reducing to L4. Do not accept L4 scope labelled
  L5 in the title.
- *Manager says the level is fixed but "we can revisit in six months":* get it in writing, with criteria.
  Promotions require scope evidence you have not yet had, so this is usually a deferral, not a
  commitment — price it accordingly at close to zero in the comparison.

**Step 4 — write it down.** Every agreement about level, scope, and review timing, in an email, so
"we'll revisit" has a written referent.

**The generalization:** the single most valuable negotiation in most searches is the level, not the
base. It is available only before the offer is written, and never again once you have accepted a
lower-level title.

## Example 4 — Full multi-offer normalization, including the work-model adjustment

**Candidate.** 11 years, senior level, two cities under consideration, three live offers.

| | **A** (large private, pre-IPO) | **B** (mid public, remote US-only) | **C** (large public, onsite) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Level / model | L5, hybrid 3 days | L4, remote | L5, onsite, downtown |
| Location (COL) | City A (100) | City B (96) | City A |
| Base | 250,000 | 215,000 | 265,000 |
| Bonus | 12% | 10% | 15% |
| Equity | 14,000 RSU @ $31 | 8,000 RSU @ $31 | 20,000 RSU @ $31 |
| Sign-on | 15,000 | 25,000 | 30,000 |
| Health | family 21,000 | employee only 8,000 | family 19,000 |
| Match | 4% / 1-yr vest | 5% / 3-yr cliff | 4% / 1-yr vest |
| PTO | 18 days + 9 hol | 15 days + 10 hol | 12 days + 9 hol |

**Year-1 cash** (one-time items × 0.65):
`A = 250,000 + 30,000 + 9,750 = 289,750` · `B = 215,000 + 21,500 + 16,250 = 252,750` ·
`C = 265,000 + 39,750 + 19,500 = 324,250`.

**COL normalization:** `A 250,000` · `B = 215,000 × (100/96) = 223,958` · `C 265,000`.

**Equity** (25% vested yr 1, × 0.70 tax, × 0.85 discount):
`A 3,500×31 = 108,500 × 0.595 = 64,558` · `B 2,000×31 = 62,000 × 0.595 = 36,890` ·
`C 5,000×31 = 155,000 × 0.595 = 92,225`.

**Benefits, annualized** (daily rate = (base+bonus)/250):
```
A: 21,000 + 250,000×0.04 = 10,000 + 18×1,120 = 20,160 + 9×1,120 = 10,080   → 61,240
B:  8,000 + 0 (3-yr cliff, not vested yr 1) + 15×946 = 14,190 + 10×946 = 9,460 → 31,650
C: 19,000 + 265,000×0.04 = 10,600 + 12×1,219 = 14,628 + 9×1,219 = 10,971   → 55,199
```

**Totals.**

| | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| Year-1 cash | 289,750 | 252,750 | 324,250 |
| Year-1 equity (net) | 64,558 | 36,890 | 92,225 |
| Benefits | 61,240 | 31,650 | 55,199 |
| **Year-1 total** | **415,548** | **321,290** | **471,674** |
| COL-adjusted base | 250,000 | 223,958 | 265,000 |

**The work-model adjustment (where the decision changes).** City A commute averages 45 min one way;
3 days × 48 weeks = 144 days × 1.5 h = **216 hours/year** ≈ 27 working days. Valued at A's daily rate
that is ~**$30,000/yr of life** — 216 hours that cannot be spent with family, exercising, or learning.
`A adjusted = 415,548 − 30,000 = 385,548` · `B = 321,290` · `C = 471,674` (12-minute downtown office).

**Three-year roll-forward** (base +5%/yr, one promotion at month 20 for A and C = +12% base and 1.6×
grant; refreshes at 25% of initial grant vesting in years 2 and 3):
```
A  Yr1 415,548 | Yr2 = 262,500 + 31,500 + (64,558+64,558) + 65,000 = 488,116
   Yr3 = 265,500 + 31,860 + 129,116 + 65,500 = 491,976   → 3-yr ≈ 1,395,640 → less ~60,000
      commute value ≈ 1,335,640
B  Yr1 321,290 | Yr2 = 225,750 + 22,575 + (36,890+36,890) + 46,000 (match now vests) = 368,105
   Yr3 = 237,040 + 23,704 + 73,780 + 47,000 = 381,524   → 3-yr ≈ 1,070,919
C  Yr1 471,674 | Yr2 = 265,000 + 39,750 + (92,225+92,225) + 57,000 = 546,200
   Yr3 = promo yr: base 296,800 + 44,520 + (92,225+92,225+8,000×31×0.595=147,560) + 60,000
         = 825,555                                              → 3-yr ≈ 1,843,429
```
**Sensitivity at share price −30% ($21.70).** Equity is ~24% of C's three-year total, so the hit is
~7%: `C ≈ 1,714,000` · `A ≈ 1,255,500` · `B ≈ 1,006,600`. **The ranking is stable under the sensitivity
that matters** — which is what makes the decision defensible: the answer does not depend on the
assumption you are least sure about.

**Non-monetary adjustments, made explicit.**
```
A  + L5 at a pre-IPO company: refresh grants may be structured well and the company is about to have
    a liquid, marked share price — real optional upside on a company you evaluated.
    − 27 days/yr of commute. − hybrid policy can change after you start.
B  + fully remote, best autonomy, US-only constraint. − one level down (compounds).
    − 3-yr cliff on the match. − equity ~57% of A's per year. − no city choice beyond the US.
C  + highest total, fastest promotion path, downtown office (12 min), weakest leave of the three.
    − onsite = least flexibility about where you live. − most concentrated bet on one stock.
```

**The decision.** C wins on money, and survives sensitivity analysis — but only after checking three
things worth more than money:
1. **Is the 12-day PTO real?** Ask the team what people actually take. If it is 12, ask for 15–18;
   leave is cheap to grant and often traded for small concessions elsewhere.
2. **What are the L6 promotion criteria?** A three-year model that assumes a promotion is only worth
   counting if the promotion is achievable.
3. **Is 20,000 in-band for L5?** If it is an exception, exceptions at entry are sometimes revisited at
   the first review — confirm in writing either way.

**Negotiation plan for C.**
```
1. Level framework and promotion criteria confirmed in writing (governs the three-year model)
2. Initial grant band confirmed; if 20,000 is above band, secure it in writing
3. PTO 12 → 15 (cheap; cash equivalent ≈ 3,700/yr at their daily rate)
4. Sign-on 30,000 → 40,000, justified by pro-rated bonus + forfeited equity
5. Base +5,000, only if 1–3 are exhausted
Leverage: "I have a live written offer at <A's level and structure> with a decision on <date A>, and an
earlier deadline at B. The scope here is my preference, so a decision is easy if the package is right."
```
**What not to do:** do not negotiate all three to the maximum simultaneously. Settle C's items 1–3,
accept C if it lands, and use A as a reference rather than as a bidding chip at every stage.

practice.reference:
**1. 🟢 Why are you leaving your current role?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
Forward-looking, never a complaint. "My work here has been good — I own X and I've learned Y. But over
the last year it has moved toward maintenance rather than the design work I want more of, and I've hit
the ceiling on what I can learn. I'm looking for a role where I'd be designing and shipping new systems,
with a team where that's the primary job." Never disparage, never hint at a conflict, never mention
compensation.

**2. 🟢 Why should we hire you?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
Shape the answer to the role's top three requirements. "Three things. First, I've done the exact
problem this role owns — at <company> I took <X> from <state> to <state> with <metric>. Second, the part
you're least staffed for is <dimension>, and that's where I've spent the last <N> years. Third, I work
the way your team works — <evidence from the posting>. Here's the project I'd point you to for each."

**3. 🟢 Tell me about yourself.** 🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**
60–90 seconds: present → relevant past → why here. "I'm a backend engineer, seven years, mostly
distributed systems and data infrastructure. Most recently at <company> I own <service>, where I <one
headline outcome>. Before that I <most relevant earlier role and outcome>. I'm applying because
<specific reason tied to this role>." Do not recite your resume; start with education only if
early-career.

**4. 🟢 Tell me about the most impactful thing you've done.** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
One project with depth: problem and why it mattered, what you chose and what you rejected, what you
built, the result with numbers, and what you would do differently. "The most consequential thing I've
done is <project>. The problem was <X>, which cost us <cost>. The obvious approach was <A> and I
rejected it because <reason>. I built <B>. The result was <metric>, and the thing I'm proudest of is
<the part nobody asks about>." That last line separates a senior answer from a mid answer.

**5. 🟡 How do you handle disagreement with a technical decision?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
Build a case, not an ego. "First I check whether we actually disagree or just see it differently —
often it's a priority mismatch, not a factual one. Then I make the disagreement cheap: a prototype, or
a measurement that would settle it. If it's genuinely a values question — consistency versus
availability — I argue the tradeoff explicitly to the person who owns the decision and commit fully
once it's made. I've been wrong more than once, which is why I try to make my wrongness cheap to
detect before I commit a team to it."

**6. 🟡 How do you handle disagreement with your manager about priorities?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
"I'll raise it once, clearly, with a recommendation rather than a problem. If the answer is still
different, I commit and execute at full strength — my job is to make their decision succeed, not to win
the argument. What I won't do is silently withdraw, because that leaves them with a broken assumption.
I'll implement it and say privately, 'I want to flag one risk so it isn't a surprise.'" Then a real
example with a good outcome.

**7. 🟡 What questions do you have for us?** 🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**
Always have three or four ready and specific: "What does success look like for the first six months?"
/ "What's the hardest technical problem the team has right now, and how much of my time would go to it?"
/ "How is on-call staffed, and what does a typical on-call week look like?" / "What's the team's
biggest source of internal disagreement right now?" / "What happened to the last person in this role?"
Never ask something you could answer from their website.

**8. 🟡 How do you decide what to work on?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
"I look for the intersection of user pain, business leverage, and something the team can finish. The
failure mode is optimizing for what's interesting to me, which is rarely what the business needs. In
practice: who is hurting, what does it cost them, and what's the smallest version that tells us whether
this is worth more. Then I bias toward work with a visible feedback loop, because work without a signal
is how teams disappear."

**9. 🟡 How do you handle an incident you're on call for?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
"Stabilize first, diagnose second, write it up third. Acknowledge, then decide whether to roll back —
my default is yes if the cause is unclear and the change is recent — communicate to the affected team
within a stated interval, and keep a real-time log because I'll need it. Then I hold every ten minutes
until the signal is clean, and I escalate only if the blast radius exceeds my authority. Afterwards I
write a blameless review with one page of actions with owners and dates, and I check that the actions
aren't the ones we already knew." Give a real example with the outcome.

**10. 🔴 How do you evaluate whether a technical decision was right, after the fact?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
"I look for whether the decision still holds under the conditions we now know about, not whether it hit
the original number. Did the load change? Did we learn the user behavior we assumed? Would I re-make it?
And if not, what specifically broke — the assumption, the estimate, or the execution? That distinction
matters, because only the first two are things better analysis would have fixed." Give an example of a
decision that was wrong and one that was right.

**11. 🟡 What separates a good engineering manager from a bad one?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
You are interviewing your future boss, so answer as someone who has been on both sides. "A good one makes
the work legible — you can tell what matters this quarter and why, and you get early warning when it
changes. They convert ambiguity into decisions instead of handing it down. They take responsibility
upward so you can focus. And they give specific feedback about your work rather than general impressions.
A bad one manages for visibility instead of outcomes, or avoids the hard conversations and lets problems
surface in reviews. The most reliable signal I use is whether people on their team volunteer for hard
projects."

**12. 🔴 How do you make technical decisions in a group?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
"I write the decision down before the meeting — problem, constraints, options, my recommendation with
reasoning, and what would make me wrong. That document does most of the work, because disagreement in a
meeting is usually about framing, not options. Then I name a decider up front, so we're solving the
problem rather than testing whose argument wins. If there's no consensus I stop arguing: I make the
call, record the reason, and set a review trigger — a metric or a date — so the decision is falsifiable
instead of permanent."

**13. 🔴 How do you handle a project that is failing?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
"Separate diagnosis from morale. First, get the facts on the timeline — when did we last have evidence
this was going to work? Then identify the class of failure: is the premise wrong, the estimate wrong, or
the execution wrong? Those have completely different responses. Then take a decision to the people
involved early, with a recommendation, because the worst outcome is a team that knows it's failing and
hasn't been told. I would rather cut scope by half and ship in two weeks than keep a full-scope plan
that misses by a year."

**14. 🔴 Your testing philosophy, and where do you disagree with the orthodoxy?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
"I test behavior, not implementation, because implementation-coupled tests make refactoring expensive
and don't tell you whether the system works. I push hardest for tests at boundaries — input validation,
error paths, concurrency, failure injection — because that's where bugs are. Where I'd push back on
orthodoxy: coverage as a target creates the illusion of safety, and mocking every collaborator produces
a suite that passes while the system fails. Integration tests with real dependencies are slower and catch
more." Give a concrete example of a test that caught a real bug.

**15. 🔴 How do you think about technical debt?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
"Debt is only debt if it has a cost that arrives later, and interest is paid in delivery speed — so the
question is always whether we're buying something. I'd rather have a system I understand with known
limitations than one I don't. I want a cost model: what does this slow down, by how much, and what would
fixing it cost. If two weeks of work removes two days from every future change, do it. If it's a quarter,
it needs a triggering event to justify it." Mention one debt you paid down and how you prioritized it.

**16. 🔴 How do you decide what to build versus buy?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
"I build when the thing is core to our differentiation, when we need to change it frequently, or when no
external option meets a hard requirement. I buy when the problem is solved well by someone whose full-time
job is solving it and I can absorb the integration cost. The failure modes are symmetric: building
something nobody wanted, and buying something we then fight constantly because we don't control the
roadmap. I also price the exit — the cost of replacing it later is part of today's decision."

**17. 🟡 How do you give and receive feedback?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
"I try to make feedback specific and close to the event — behavior, observed, impact — and I'd rather
hear something uncomfortable early than useful and late. As a receiver I ask 'what did you expect?' and
treat the gap between expectation and result as the actual feedback, not the conclusion. The failure mode
I work on is that when I'm tired or defensive I hear the conclusion and ignore the reasoning." Give a
real example of feedback you received that changed your behavior, and one you gave that landed.

**18. 🟡 How do you stay current in your field?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
"I have three filters. I follow a small number of people whose work I respect, I read the primary source
— design docs, RFCs, post-mortems — rather than the summary, and I try to apply what I read to something
within a couple of weeks, because reading without application doesn't stick. I'd rather go deep on one
new thing a quarter than skim ten." Be honest about what you currently read; vagueness is a red flag.

**19. 🔴 Tell me about a time you missed a deadline or shipped something that failed.** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
An integrity question. "I committed to <X> by <date> and missed it. Here's what happened: <cause,
without blaming>. Here's the recovery I did: <honest recovery>. Here's what I changed: <system change>."
Then what you learned about estimating. A candidate who has never missed a deadline is either very new
or not being honest. Do not offer a disguised strength.

**20. 🔴 Tell me about a time you were wrong about a technical judgment.** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
Give a specific position, why you held it, the evidence that changed your mind, what it cost, and what
you do now. "I argued we didn't need to shard <service> until <number> users. I was wrong — the cost
wasn't write throughput, it was the operational complexity of migrations we had to do by hand. What I
took from it: I now distinguish 'scaling limits' from 'operational limits', because they have different
solutions, and I check for the second when I look at a system's growth."

**21. 🟡 Why are you at the level you're at, rather than the one above?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
The best signal you can give a senior interviewer. "The next level for me is <scope across teams,
leading a migration, owning a roadmap>. What I have is <specific evidence>. What I don't have yet is
<specific, honest>. If you hire me for the level above, here's what I'd do in the first six months to
earn it — <plan>." Candidates who claim they already operate at the level above are routinely filtered
out in the calibration conversation afterwards.

**22. 🔴 How would you scope and staff a 30-person, 6-month project?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
"First I'd find out whether the six months is real, because I'd rather negotiate the scope than discover
in month five that the date was aspirational. Then define the one outcome that makes this successful if
everything else slips, and build toward that first so we have something shippable by week eight. On
staffing, I'd want two or three people who know the domain deeply and a couple who know the new
technology, deliberately paired, and a dedicated point person for coordination rather than assuming a
senior engineer picks it up. And I'd plan the last two weeks for hardening and rollout, because that's
where every project I've watched slip decided its outcome." Then a real project and what happened.

**23. 🔴 Your system is degrading. What do you do in the first hour?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
"Minute one: confirm what's actually happening and whether users are affected, using two independent
signals — a single dashboard can be lying. If users are affected I declare an incident and get a second
person on it immediately, because solo debugging is how an hour becomes three. The first three moves, in
order: check for a recent change, check whether a dependency is degraded, check whether it's capacity or
correctness. Those three cover most causes. Everything after that is diagnosis, and I'll be explicit in
updates about what I don't know rather than guessing. I'll also set the rollback criteria before I need
them." Then a real example and the actual cause.

**24. 🔴 How do you handle a dependency you don't control?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
"Three stages. First, reduce the blast radius: timeouts, circuit breakers, retries with jitter and a
budget, bulkheads, and caching that respects their SLO rather than ours. Second, change what we ask for:
better terms, a dedicated path, a version, a deprecation notice. Third, plan for the worst: our
replacement or forked path, and how long it would take. The most common failure is spending all the
engineering effort on retries, which converts a dependency outage into our own outage — retries need
budgets specifically so a slow dependency can't consume our whole thread pool."

**25. 🟡 What salary are you looking for?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
Never answer first if you can avoid it: "Can I ask how the band is structured for this level, and where
my experience lands in it? I'd rather get the whole package right." If forced, give a range at the top
of what is credible, anchored to scope and market, with the reasoning attached: "For this scope I expect
<L+1>, and for total cash in the <X–Y> range. I'd have flexibility on structure." Then stop talking.
Never name your current salary.

**26. 🟡 What's your biggest weakness?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
Real, non-fatal, with a demonstrated mitigation. "I used to over-invest in getting a design perfect before
showing anyone — I'd hold a proposal for weeks. What I do now is show work in progress deliberately
early, at a level where I ask for direction rather than approval, because I got burned by a design I was
proud of that solved a problem nobody had." Avoid the "I work too hard" lie and disguised strengths. Be
ready for "tell me about a time."

**27. 🔴 Why should we not hire you?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
Integrity and self-awareness; a bad answer sinks a strong candidate. "Two reasons someone might decide
against me. I sometimes over-index on the technical depth of a solution and under-invest in the social
work of getting people behind it — I've learned to do that deliberately and early, and to ask for help.
And my background is <domain>, so in <adjacent domain> I'd be learning for the first few months where
someone with <domain> experience would be productive day one. If this role needs day-one productivity
in <adjacent domain>, I might not be right. If it needs someone who reaches production quality fast in
<domain>, I would." Then what you would do to fix each.

**28. 🔴 What do you want to be doing in three years?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
Tie it to the role and to real scope. "I want to be leading a system or area where I'm responsible for
design across more than one team, and being the person people come to when the hard design question is
<your domain>. I'm not in a rush to manage people — I've done it and I'm good at it, but I'd rather go
deep a couple more years and then decide." Then connect it: "That's why I'm talking to you, because
<specific reason>."

**29. 🟡 Why this company?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
Never answer about mission generically. Use one of three real reasons: a specific technical problem you
want to be near, a domain you want deeper, or a constraint you find interesting rather than merely
acceptable. "I read your post on <specific technical thing> and hit a related version of the same problem
at <current company> — <the specific thing>. I'd like to be working on that class of problem rather
than one layer away from it. And the constraint that <their system has> is one I enjoy, because
<reason>." Finish with something you want to learn from them specifically.

**30. 🔴 Anything you want us to know before we decide?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
Close gaps, raise unmentioned evidence, or flag logistics. "Two things. First, I noticed your posting
asks for <X> — I haven't worked in production with it, but here's the adjacent thing I did do
<specific work>, and I'd pick it up fast; I'd rather you hear that from me than find out in week six.
Second, my availability is <date>, and I'm in the process at <other company> with a decision on <real
date>, so if there's timeline pressure I'd rather we plan around it openly."

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**The core claim.** Most employers do not "read" your resume; they parse it into structured fields
and then a recruiter or filter queries that record. Your resume is a source for a database row.

**Parse pipeline:** detect format (column count, tables); segment regions (contact, experience,
education, skills, free text); extract fields by regex against known labels; extract entities
(companies, titles, schools) and normalize titles into an internal taxonomy; reconstruct date
ranges from several formats; tokenize and index content words; score the record against a
requisition or keyword query, and threshold decides pass/fail.

**The eight failures:**

| Failure | Mechanism | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Multi-column layout | Text assigned to wrong region; bullets land in a skills bucket | Single column; two-column header only |
| Header/footer content | Parsers commonly exclude running headers entirely | No contact info in document headers |
| Text boxes and shapes | Not in the linear text flow; often invisible | Never |
| Tables for layout | Reading order interleaves cells | Tables only for real tabular data |
| Images of text | No text layer at all | Text as text, no logos |
| Ruling lines in content | Used as region separators, producing false splits | No horizontal rules inside content |
| Non-standard date formats | Date heuristics miss them | `Mon YYYY` consistently |
| Custom field labels | Dumped into free text or dropped | Use `Experience`, `Education`, `Skills` |

**The invisible failure** is not rejection but *silent truncation*: the record looks fine while two
of four jobs are missing or your skills block landed inside your summary field. It surfaces as "I
have your resume" followed by questions about things you did not write, or a request to "reformat."
Treat that as a parse failure report.

**How to verify.** Paste the submitted file into a plain-text editor and read it top to bottom;
anything out of order, duplicated, or missing is what the parser may have seen. Then upload to a
free parser and read the *dumped fields*, not the visual rendering, because the rendering is a
reconstruction.

**Design rule.** Every item must be locatable by keyword query without human interpretation. If your
most differentiating work cannot be found by a keyword, it will not be found by a search. Rewrite for
retrieval first, then for humans.

**What ATS does *not* do.** Systems generally do not auto-reject you for formatting; humans reject
for content. Formatting matters because of downstream effects — truncation, misfiled skills,
invisible content — not because a machine dislikes your fonts. Do not sacrifice clarity to satisfy
a parser you have not tested.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**

**Canonical structure.** One column. One page under ten relevant years, two above or where depth is
required. No graphics. Section labels a recruiter's filter already knows.

1. **Header** — name, city + country, email, phone with country code if international, LinkedIn,
   GitHub, portfolio if genuinely strong. Plain text, no icons, in the body not the document header.
2. **Summary (3–4 lines, optional)** — role, years, the two domains you are strongest in, scale or
   context. Present tense. Skip it if the top third of the page already answers the reader's question.
3. **Experience (60–70% of page one)** — reverse chronological; company, title, location, dates on
   one line, then 3–5 bullets per role, strongest first.
4. **Skills** — grouped by category (languages, frameworks, data stores, infrastructure, practices)
   because that is how recruiters search. Only what you can be interviewed on: "listed" means
   "discussable."
5. **Education** — degree, institution, field, dates; coursework or honors only if relevant.
6. **Optional** — Publications, Patents, Open Source, Speaking, Certifications. Only if populated.

**Bullet anatomy.**
```
<Strong verb> <what you built or changed>, <how: mechanism/technique>, <measurable outcome>.
```
Three clauses, three readers: the keyword filter needs verb and nouns, the skim-reader needs the
*what*, the interview needs the outcome. Outcomes are mandatory at senior and staff level.

**Length per role.** Junior: 3–4 roles. Mid (3–8 yrs): 3–4. Senior (8–15): 4–5. Staff+: 4–6 with
early ones compressed to one line each, optionally plus a "Selected Impact" block above Experience so
strongest outcomes are visible without scrolling.

**Details.** Dates as `Jul 2023 – Present` so tenure is computable. Titles as held; if yours is
unrecognizable, keep it and add a clarifier — silent title upgrades fail the first screen call and
destroy trust permanently. File as text-selectable PDF with embedded fonts, named
`FirstnameLastname-Resume-<Role>.pdf`, because recruiters forward by filename. No tracked changes,
comments, hidden text, or keyword-stuffing footer.

**Ordering.** Recruiters read Z and F patterns; put your strongest content in the upper-right and
center band, never the weakest in the first third, and never break a page mid-bullet.

**What to cut.** Bullets describing duties ("responsible for maintaining CI pipelines"). Skills older
than three years you would not discuss. Self-assessment adjectives. Anything you cannot defend in a
technical screen.

**Red flags.** Unexplained gaps, job-hopping patterns, every bullet starting with the same verb, a
summary that restates the title, and a skills list too long to be a claim list. Fine once each;
together they read as sloppiness.

**Versioning.** Master plus per-role variants, tracked in the same table as applications (15.2.4).
Never send the master.

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**The rule.** A number must be true, attributable to your work directly or as a clear contributor,
and defensible when probed. If you cannot source it, do not include it. False precision is worse
than no number because it invites the follow-up that ends the process.

**The quantification ladder.**
1. Directly measured, yours: "Cut p99 checkout latency from 2.4 s to 380 ms."
2. Measured, shared credit stated: "…as part of a 4-person team." Name team size for shared work.
3. Derived, with the derivation shown: "Reduced index 9 GB → 1.2 GB, cutting instance cost ~38%."
4. Bounded estimate with basis: "Roughly 3× throughput, estimated from load tests, not production."
5. Ordinal without a number: "Reduced latency enough to clear the internal SLO we missed at peak."
6. Qualitative, for genuinely non-numeric value: "Made the deploy pipeline safe to run on demand."

**Never convert a team's number into a personal number.** The most common resume lie is not
fabrication but silent ownership transfer. `Led migration of 40 services` when you owned the tooling
is misleading; `Built the migration tooling used across a 40-service migration` is not.

**Numbers to reach for when nothing looks numeric:** *time* (latency, build time, time to first
deploy, incident time-to-mitigate, manual work removed); *money* (infra cost, vendor spend, revenue
protected — most persuasive because it maps to budget); *scale* (requests/sec, data volume,
tenants, messages/sec); *reliability* (error rate, availability, SLO attainment, MTTR, pages per
on-call week); *volume of change* (PRs, releases, migrations, tests added); *human* (engineers
enabled, tickets deflected, runbooks); *process* (review turnaround, commit-to-production lead
time, percent of deploys automated); *growth* (adoption percentage, percent of traffic migrated).

**Instrument your impact before you need it.** Treat the current job as an evidence-collection
project: record the baseline before you start; record the after-state at each shipped slice; ask
users what changed for them — that yields scale numbers you cannot instrument yourself; keep a
private note of problem, baseline, action, after, who said so, where the dashboard lives.

**Claiming credit with words.** "Owned X" (single accountable engineer); "Built X; used by N teams";
"Co-led X with 3 others"; "Contributed to X" but name the component you owned; "Designed the
approach for X; two engineers implemented it under my design" — senior impact, accurate framing.

**Formatting.** Write `38%`, `2.4 s`, `$1.2M`, `9 GB` — space between value and unit, no unicode
tricks. Digits are indexable, words are not.

**Sanity check.** For each number: where did it come from, who could verify it, would a colleague
agree with this sentence? Vague answers mean weaken or delete. Then ask whether the magnitude is
plausible to a domain expert — `94% cost reduction` invites the skepticism a realistic result
avoids. Prefer absolute values to bare percentages: "p99 of 380 ms at 4k rps" still means something
in three years; "300% improvement" means nothing.

Explain the four framings you will actually need and when you would use it.
Explain the reframe procedure and when you would use it.
Explain bucket — assign each to a target framing. projects in two buckets are often your and when you would use it.
Explain the three-sentence summary and when you would use it.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**The claim.** You need at least two framings of the same experience, written from reusable blocks
rather than authored fresh each time. Same facts, different selection and emphasis. Never different
claims.

**The four framings you will actually need.** *Backend/systems*: latency, throughput, storage,
consistency, failure modes, cost. *Frontend/product*: interaction latency, accessibility,
conversion-relevant metrics, design-system leverage, testing strategy. *Data/ML*: dataset scale,
pipeline reliability, model quality, evaluation methodology, inference cost, lineage.
*Infrastructure/platform*: provisioning time, fleet efficiency, developer experience metrics,
observability coverage, incident reduction, tooling adoption.

**The reframe procedure.**
1. **Inventory** — every role as a list of projects, noting each project's dominant domain.
2. **Bucket** — assign each to a target framing. Projects in two buckets are often your
   differentiator, not a problem.
3. **Select** — per framing, keep relevant and adjacent projects, ordered by relevance to the job's
   first three requirements.
4. **Re-derive bullets** — same achievement in target-domain vocabulary. One project's UI work is a
   frontend bullet; its data-layer work is a backend bullet. Two true sentences, no contradiction.
5. **Rewrite the summary** — the highest-leverage single edit in the document.
6. **Reorder skills** — target stack to the front. Reordering is free and moves keyword rankings.

**The three-sentence summary.**
```
<Role you are applying for> with <N> years in <primary domain>.
Focused on <two specific technical areas where you have real depth>.
Most recent results: <one headline outcome>, <one outcome>.
```
Its job is to make the reader's next question obviously answerable from the rest of the page. If
the third sentence does not fit the target role, use a different recent outcome.

**How many variants.** Two or three written carefully beat ten written lazily. A practical set:
`backend-systems`, `data-ml`, `frontend-product`, plus a `general`. Manage as one master with a
documented include/exclude map per variant, which keeps them from drifting into inconsistency —
interviewers do catch a project described two ways in two rounds.

**Consistency rules, enforced.** Dates, titles, and company names identical everywhere. Any metric
cited in one variant may be cited in any other. Your narrative of each project stable across
rounds, screens, and references.

**Tailoring to a posting — three things only.** Mirror their terminology where accurate. Reorder
the top third so their first-listed requirements are answered first. Add or foreground the one
project mapping to their most distinctive requirement. Resist further edits; over-tailoring burns
time and introduces inconsistency risk.

**Requirement extraction from the JD.** Classify every requirement as satisfied-and-proven,
satisfied-adjacent, or not-satisfied. Move proven items into the top third; convert adjacent items
to honest framing ("worked with X extensively; Y only at prototype scale"). Never claim the third
category — interviewers find the gap in round one, and the cost of that discovery far exceeds the
cost of not claiming it.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain signal hierarchy and when you would use it.
Explain profile readme — highest leverage, lowest effort and when you would use it.
Explain pinned repo selection rule and when you would use it.
Explain repository presentation checklist and when you would use it.
Explain commit and pr hygiene and when you would use it.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**

**Signal hierarchy.** Pinned repositories (quality always), profile README, contribution
consistency, authorship in repos you name, issue and review participation, then profile
completeness. Stars are near-irrelevant alone — a repo with 4 stars, a real README, and tests
signals more than 800 stars of tutorial code.

**Profile README — highest leverage, lowest effort.** In order: one line naming who you are and
what you work on, parsable by a non-specialist; what you are currently learning or building; three
pinned repos with one-line descriptions and why each is pinned; optionally seeking status *only*
while actively searching; contact links. Under 60 lines.

**Pinned repo selection rule.** Your strongest single project (real, non-tutorial, tests, green CI,
README explaining problem and design); your most *relevant* project for the role you want even if
smaller; and one demonstrating a different dimension — performance, tooling, a usable library.
Never pin a repo with no README, no license, or a `TODO` as the first thing a reader sees.

**Repository presentation checklist.** README opens with the problem in two or three sentences a
non-author understands. Then "why this exists / who it is for" with explicit non-goals; architecture
or design with a diagram and primary data flow; a Quickstart you verified recently; a status section
(supported / experimental / archived) that reads as maturity signal; **design decisions and
tradeoffs including what you would change differently** — this single section disproportionately
signals senior and staff competence; a license; tests with a green CI badge.

**Commit and PR hygiene.** Review your contribution graph before sharing: sparse clustered activity
reads better than fabricated consistency, and a wall of green is more suspicious than a dip.
Conventional commits, small PRs with substantive descriptions, prompt responses to review, no
force-push over reviewed branches, no self-merging without review on projects you want taken
seriously.

**Profile completeness.** Photo if comfortable; a bio that is role plus domain; location, employer,
pins; and a commit email you will still have in two years. Custom URL as a name-based URL, which
survives job changes.

**What to remove.** Tutorial repos from 2019. Forks you never touched. Anything containing secrets,
credentials, or legacy code you would not want read — audit before sharing, not after.

**Green graph discipline.** Do not manufacture activity. It does not survive five minutes of skilled
repo browsing, and hiring managers who browse notice the gap between a busy profile and repos with
one commit and no tests.

**Interview ammunition.** Before each interview, note the two repos you can discuss in depth, the
specific design decisions, and one thing you would change. "Let me walk you through the retry
design in `src/queue/consumer.ts`" is a materially different signal from a technology list.

**Confidential-work hygiene.** Never publish employer code, internal documents, data, or dashboard
screenshots. Abstract the lesson; build a clean-room equivalent. This is both legal and a signal —
interviewers notice suspiciously vague "I worked on internal things."

---

Explain what a strong project demonstrates, in priority order and when you would use it.
Explain the readme skeleton and when you would use it.
Explain why "limitations" disproportionately matters and when you would use it.
Explain depth beats breadth, always and when you would use it.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**The strategic point.** A portfolio project's job is to let someone evaluate your judgment without
your presence. So the artifact must make *decisions* visible, not just functionality. Code that
runs is table stakes; a documented rationale is the signal.

**What a strong project demonstrates, in priority order:** judgment under constraints (you chose an
approach and can say why, including what you rejected); depth in one area (performance, concurrency,
storage, type systems, numerical code); operational maturity (tests, CI, observability, error
handling, deployment); scope control — a small finished coherent thing beats three half-built ones.

**The README skeleton.**
```
# Project name
One line: what it is and who it is for.
## Why            The problem, concretely. Numbers if you have them.
## Demo           Screenshot, GIF, or live link. Demo > code.
## Design         Architecture prose + diagram. Components. Primary data flow. Storage model.
## Key decisions  ### Decision 1: <choice> over <alternative> — context, options, tradeoffs,
                 what we gave up.
## Performance    Methodology, workload, results table. What was measured and how.
## Testing        Unit, integration, property, load. What is and is not covered.
## Limitations    Explicit non-goals. Senior reviewers read this first.
## Running it     Prerequisites, commands, expected output. Verified recently.
```
**Why "Limitations" disproportionately matters.** Naming what your system does not do proves you
know what it does. Candidates who hide limitations read as junior; a reviewer reading a limitations
section infers competence, because only someone who understands the system can enumerate its edges.

**Depth beats breadth, always.** One repo with 3,000 thoughtful lines, real tests, and a design
document beats nine CRUD apps. If breadth must be shown, use one tiny project per domain with a very
short README stating the decision and the lesson, labeled an exercise.

**Ideas that map to roles.** *Backend/distributed*: a consistent log; a rate limiter with a
documented algorithm and failure semantics; a task queue with at-least-once delivery and idempotency;
a KV store with persistence; an LSM tree; a distributed counter. *Data/ML*: a reproducible pipeline
with versioned data; an evaluation harness with offline metrics and a stated failure mode; a
streaming join. *Frontend*: a virtualized list with measured performance; an accessible date picker; a
state layer with time travel; a design system with documented tokens. *Platform/SRE*: IaC for a
small environment; a golden-signal dashboard; a chaos harness; CI with caching and measured
improvement. *Systems/security*: a TLS implementation; a password hasher benchmark; a capability-
based auth model; a fuzzer harness for your own parser.

**Instrumentation as the differentiator.** Include a benchmarks directory, a load-test script, and a
results table with methodology — hardware, workload shape, warm-up, iterations, variance. Publishing
the methodology is what makes it credible and almost no candidate does it correctly.

**Test quality signals.** Boundary and error-path tests; property-based tests where appropriate; tests
that would fail if the implementation were subtly wrong; no giant mock temples; a suite a stranger
can run. Do not chase a coverage number.

**Deployed beats local-only.** If you can host it cheaply, deploy it and put the live link first.
Verify it still runs before every interview cycle; a dead demo link is worse than none. Then run one
keyboard-only pass — a frontend reviewer finds an unusable site in ninety seconds.

**Do not build during your search.** Building portfolio projects while interviewing consumes the
hours you need for outreach and prep. Build before the search or after you have an offer. If you
build now, cap it at two weeks and make it small and finished.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**

**What LinkedIn is actually good for,** in value order: recruiter searchability (recruiters run
boolean keyword searches with title and location filters, and your headline and About are indexed
more reliably than your experience bullets); inbound from warm contacts; and social proof of
activity. Viral posts, connection counts, and engagement hacking produce no interviews.

**Headline — the highest-leverage 200 characters.** Most people waste it on their job title.
```
<Role> · <Domain depth> · <Scale or domain you operate at> · <Second language or skill>
```
Shape: `Backend Engineer · Distributed systems & data infrastructure · Sub-ms latency at high
throughput · Go, Rust, Kafka`. Include the words recruiters filter on: role, domain, 2–4
technologies you actually want to be found for.

**About section — write 15 lines, not 5.** What you do in plain language (1); the two problems you
are best at solving (2–4); three specific accomplishments with numbers (5–9); stack and practices
(10–12); what you want next plus contact, or if not searching, what you are building (13–15). First
person, plain sentences, no buzzword stacking ("synergy", "leveraging", "dynamic professional").

**Experience entries mirror your resume.** Same titles, dates, bullets. Inconsistency reads as
carelessness and can be caught in reference checks. Add a line describing the company and what the
team owned, which helps a recruiter unfamiliar with it.

**Skills: order matters.** Pin your top ten. Add the ones you want to be found for even if you rate
yourself lower — the field is a targeting tool, not a self-assessment, and recruiters filter on it.

**Featured section: use it.** Best project, best writing, your site, your résumé. It is what a
visitor sees first after About and what converts a profile visit into real evaluation. Empty
Featured on a senior profile is conspicuous.

**Custom URL.** Name-based, so it survives job changes and looks professional when printed on a CV.

**Open to Work settings.** Recruiter visibility on, with role types, locations, and remote preference
specified.

**Connection requests.** Personalize with one line of actual context and the reason you want to talk.
Never mass-request with a pitch attached — it damages your name with the exact people whose referrals
you want.

**Posting.** Post when you have something useful and can sustain it: a technical insight with a
concrete number, a lessons-learned post-mortem, a strong disagreement with a popular idea, a
curated reading list with commentary. Two posts a month beats daily engagement bait. Never post
company-confidential content.

**Recommendations.** Ask former colleagues rather than managers you still work under, and give them
three specific bullet points to build on — the request matters more than the ask.

**Privacy hygiene.** No confidential project detail for your employer. No publicly posted salary
expectations. Know who can see your uploaded résumé. Fix order for one hour: headline, About,
Featured, skills order, custom URL.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Why it works as signal.** OSS demonstrates working inside *someone else's* constraints: reading
unfamiliar code, matching conventions, negotiating design in review, being correct in a codebase you
do not control. That is a different and more valuable claim than "I built three projects."

**Five contribution types, easiest to hardest.** Documentation fixes — typos, broken links, missing
examples, unclear explanations; real and universally underestimated. Reproducible bug reports — minimal
repro, environment, actual vs expected, logs, proposed fix; underrated because maintainers value them.
Test additions — untested edge cases, regression tests, coverage gaps in a module you use. Small
features and bug fixes — real code in an unfamiliar codebase. Design and API work — deprecations,
boundary refactors, RFCs; high value, high effort, high rejection rate.

**Choosing a project.** Start from tools you already depend on, so you understand the constraints and
keep using the result. Then filter for: active recently with responsive maintainers; a
`CONTRIBUTING.md` and code of conduct; `good first issue` or `help wanted` labels; small enough that
your PR will not be ignored by volume.

**The first-contribution path that works.**
1. Read `CONTRIBUTING.md`, the code of conduct, and the templates. Fully.
2. Install and build the project. Do this first — it is the real work and the most common reason
   first PRs stall.
3. Read the code near your target area and the recent commit history to learn conventions.
4. **Claim the issue before writing code:** "I'd like to take this — here's my approach." This one
   step dramatically increases acceptance and avoids duplicate effort.
5. Open a draft PR early for large changes, to get design feedback before writing it all.
6. Keep the change small and single-purpose; resist "while I was in there" edits.
7. Match commit format, test framework, and linting; run the project's own checks.
8. Write the PR description: problem, change, how you tested, issue closed.
9. Respond to review promptly; push back with data, never be defensive about style.

**Sustaining — the compounding strategy.** After one accept, switch to maintenance mode on a project
you already touched: one issue, one PR review, or one doc fix every few weeks. This keeps your
contribution visible, keeps your setup alive, and grows your review reputation, which is the actual
currency. A long tail of small contributions to one project beats scattered one-offs across ten.

**Advancing to reviewer.** Review is where your judgment becomes visible and maintainers notice you.
Review correctness first, style second, and always distinguish "this is wrong" from "I would have
done this differently." Reviews are public artifacts whether you want them or not.

**Time management.** Two to four hours a week, and not during peak interview season. A stalled PR is
a negative artifact; a small finished one is positive. If pausing, say so or close the PR with a note.

**Employed engineers.** Never contribute to a library that competes with your employer's product
without checking your agreement, and never during work hours to anything that could be construed as
your job.

**What to put on a resume.** Name the project, your role, and one outcome: "Contributed 12 fixes
and 3 features to `<project>`; now triage reviewer for its `<subsystem>`." The *kind* of change
signals level better than a raw count.

**The timing truth.** OSS history compounds over months to years. Starting during a search is
usually too slow to matter for that search — which makes it the highest-leverage thing to start now
so it is available in the next one.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Why writing still works.** A good post is a compressed, verifiable demonstration of thinking: you
chose an approach, you know why, you measured it, you can explain it. It compounds — a post written
once is read for years, a resume bullet is read once. And it gives you something specific to send a
recruiter, the best cold-outreach hook available (15.2.3).

**What gets read and shared.** *Debugging narratives* — real problem, wrong hypothesis, actual root
cause, fix, and what monitoring caught it; readers love these because they are honest. *Deep dives
on one mechanism* — how a protocol, algorithm, storage engine, or distributed-systems guarantee
works, with diagrams and a worked example. *Comparisons with methodology* — benchmarks with stated
workload and tradeoffs, always with a "this is what my workload looked like" caveat. *Migration and
refactoring write-ups* — before state, target state, why, rollout, what broke, what you would do
differently. *"Here is what I got wrong"* — rare and disproportionately valued. *Pragmatic
operational posts* — deploys, incident review, on-call load.

**What does not get read.** Framework listicles. "10 things about X" without depth. Tutorials
restating documentation. Hot takes with no evidence. Career advice from people with no track record.
Anything that reads as content marketing.

**Structures that work.** *Post-mortem*: context → symptom → timeline → hypotheses tried → root
cause → fix → detection improvement → what I'd do earlier. *Mechanism explainer*: problem → mental
model → diagram → algorithm → complexity → worked example → failure modes → where the abstraction
breaks. *Comparison*: question → constraints → candidates → methodology → results → interpretation →
what I chose and why → when your answer would differ. *Tutorial that assumes competence*: explain
what the documentation does not.

**Cadence.** One substantial post a month beats a weekly micro-post. Keep a backlog of questions
people actually ask you — those topics are pre-validated. Draft in private, publish on a schedule you
can sustain, and never publish an argument you would not defend in review.

**Distribution is part of the work.** Post to your site, cross-post a condensed version to LinkedIn
with a link, share in the relevant community, and send contacts the *direct link* — not "look at my
blog."

**Confidentiality.** No employer code, no uncleared internal numbers, no colleague-identifying
anecdotes without consent. Abstract the lesson; keep specifics generic. Getting this wrong is a
career-ending kind of mistake, and being careful is itself a signal.

**Measuring whether it works.** Count quality engagement — thoughtful replies, inbound messages
referencing a specific post, DMs from engineers — not raw views. Ten readers who respect you beat ten
thousand impressions.

**Using posts in interviews.** Send one relevant post with a follow-up, not as a substitute for being
qualified. Referencing your own writing as evidence of depth is natural; sending it unprompted as
proof of skill is not. And editor relationships are a medium-term play — one well-placed relationship
can produce a platform-level audience.
