🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Opening frame — never name a number first.**
> "I'm glad we're at this stage. Before we talk about specifics, I'd like to make sure we're aligned
> on scope and level, because that's what everything else keys off. Can you walk me through how you
> see the role and where it's leveled?"

**Level conversation.**
> "Based on the scope — owning X end to end, with Y and Z teams as partners — my experience lines up
> with <level> rather than <level>. How does leveling work here, and who would I need to convince?
> Here's the work that supports it: <two concrete examples, one with a result>."

**When asked "what are you looking for?"**
> "Before I answer — can I ask how the band is structured for this level, and where my experience
> sits inside it? I'd rather optimize for the whole package and for the role being correctly leveled
> than negotiate one line item."

**If you must give a number.**
> "For base, I'm targeting the top of what's approved for this level given the scope, and I have
> flexibility on structure. For total cash with the target bonus, that puts me around <range>. And
> I'd expect the equity grant to be sized for the level we settle on."

**Naming a competing offer.**
> "I have a written offer at <level> with <structure>, and I want to be straightforward that it's
> active. The scope here is what I care most about and the total package is comparable. If you can
> move on the areas below, I'd have difficulty saying no."

Truth only. "Active" means the deadline is real. Never fabricate a competing offer — the details are
easy to verify and the consequence is permanent.

**The ask, as a package.**
> "Here's what would let me say yes quickly. First, base at <X>, top of the band for the scope.
> Second, the initial grant at <N> shares, sized to the level. Third, a signing bonus of <amount>
> covering what I forfeit leaving now. Fourth, an off-cycle review at <month> tied to scope. If base
> is fixed, I'm open to moving the one-time components instead."

**Signing bonus justification.**
> "The amount is the one-time forfeiture: my target bonus pro-rated for the year plus the unvested
> equity I can't take with me, which comes to <amount>. If cash isn't workable, an equivalent
> one-time equity grant is fine. Can you check with <approver>? I can put the argument in writing."

**Base justification that is not about your needs.**
> "My current base is <X>, but I don't want to anchor there, so let me give you the market picture:
> for this scope and level in <market> I'm seeing <range> based on <specific sources>. I'm asking for
> the top of that because of the <specific depth> work — the <thing> migration and the <thing>
> reliability work are directly relevant to what this team is solving."

**When base cannot move.**
> "I understand base is fixed at this level. Would the company be open to a one-time equity top-up,
> or a signing bonus to make me whole on the forfeiture? Those are the two that would bridge the gap."

**When they ask what would make you say yes.**
> "If you can get me to <X> on base, or equivalent on the package, I'm in. I'm not going to hold out
> for something I don't think exists — I want to work here."

**Response to "we don't have room."**
> "Understood. What *is* flexible? If it's helpful, here's what I could work with: <specific trade>
> for <specific trade>. I have flexibility on <X>."

**Post-offer, still deciding.**
> "I want to be thoughtful, and honest: I have another process at a similar level with a decision
> point on <date>. I'm evaluating you very seriously — could you get me the final terms by <date>?"

**Declining with grace.**
> "I've decided to go with <other company>. I want you to hear it from me first because you've been
> straightforward. Thank you for <specific thing>. If your search ever needs a <your skill>, call me."

**Escalating to the hiring manager.**
> "I'd like to talk through two things, both about the role rather than money: how the scope is
> leveled, and where the team expects this hire to go in the first year. Does the number change if
> the scope is what I described?"

**Ask about titles carefully.** Titles vary by convention and cost nothing, so companies grant them more
freely than money — but some promotions trigger comp review, some titles are reserved, and a "principal"
title implying the wrong level creates administrative problems. Ask whether the title is level-mapped.

**Silence is a tool.** After you make your case, stop talking. The other side frequently fills the gap
with something you did not expect.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**What a counter offer is.** Your current employer matching part or all of a new offer to keep you.
Common, and less useful than candidates hope.

**Why it usually fails.** (1) You have already decided — counters work when genuinely undecided, and once
you have accepted elsewhere your commitment is visible and trust is broken. (2) The money treats the
symptom — the reason you wanted to leave is rarely salary, and a counter that does not address the
underlying problem postpones the exit. (3) The match is incomplete — frequently base but not equity, or
this year but not next, discovered after you have resigned. (4) Trust is damaged — many managers see
an offer-accepting-then-returning employee as a flight risk, and some deals become "we promoted you but
we will be reviewing you carefully." (5) It is a bridge with a cost — you will likely leave again from a
weaker position having burned goodwill, and the second search is harder. (6) Internal equity breaks —
being raised to a level others see you as may expose you in the next reorganization. (7) Timing —
counters arrive late, compressing your decision window, and the raise often lands in a closed budget cycle.

**Where counter offers are best.** When you have not yet decided and the current job is genuinely
attractive; when the gap is small and specific and you can articulate what the raise would fix; when the
offer being countered is lateral with no growth; and when the real problem was one specific fixable
thing — a bad project, a missing mentor, a stalled promotion — and the company addresses *that*.

**Evaluate a counter offer seriously.** Is it permanent or a one-time retention payment that expires if
you leave within a window — a bribe with a timer? Does it change title and level, or only the number? Is
it accompanied by real scope change? Is it paid from a budget that could be clawed back or contingent on a
rating? What happens if you decline, and who knows you negotiated? Does it come with an implied longer
tenure?

**The conversation.** Be direct, brief, and honest.
> "I want to be straightforward: I've been offered <X> and have until <date> to decide. I've thought
> seriously about staying, because I like <specific thing>. But <specific problem> is what led me to
> look, and a number alone doesn't change that. I'm open to talking about what would change it — but
> I want to be honest that I can't commit without that."

**If you take a counter.** Leave in writing with a respectful notice, thank them, and stay committed for
at least six months if you can. Then plan the real exit with the same discipline. If the counter resolved
nothing structural, you are in a worse market position than when you started, having re-established
loyalty you did not feel.

**The ethical dimension.** Accepting a counter after accepting another offer is a legitimate business
decision but breaks a commitment to someone who made you an offer. Do it only when genuinely torn and the
counter addresses a real reason for leaving. Tell the other company promptly and courteously either way.

**Prevention.** If a counter is likely, keep the search quiet, do not discuss your intentions broadly, and
do not let enthusiasm for leaving leak. But do not lie if asked directly — that ends the relationship
permanently. **The generalization:** counter offers are a symptom of a weak internal alternative. Build
one — a promotion case, a role change, a transfer, a manager conversation with a deadline.

Equity-adjacent value that is easy to miss

Explain health insurance — evaluate the plan, not the contribution and when you would use it.
Explain retirement and when you would use it.
Explain equity-adjacent value that is easy to miss and when you would use it.
Explain work-model benefits and when you would use it.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Why this deserves attention.** Benefits can be worth five to fifteen percent of total compensation,
they are often negotiable in aggregate when the company wants you, and the highest-value items are not in
the offer letter.

**Health insurance — evaluate the plan, not the contribution.** What matters: employer contribution
amount and whether it is a flat subsidy or a percentage of premium; plan type (HMO, PPO, HDHP, EPO) and
network breadth where you actually live; deductible, out-of-pocket maximum, and coinsurance — the numbers
that determine what a serious illness costs you; family coverage cost and whether dependent premiums are
subsidized; prescription, mental health, fertility and family-forming coverage, which vary enormously and
are a real quality-of-life difference; and HSA eligibility — a high-deductible plan with an HSA
contribution is excellent for a healthy person and terrible for a chronic-condition household, which is a
genuine calculation, not a preference. Also check network adequacy where you live and whether your
doctors are in-network; surprise bills and out-of-network denials are a real financial risk. Method: get
the plan's summary of benefits and coverage, compute your expected annual cost plus your worst case, and
compare those numbers across offers in money, not by plan name.

**Retirement.** Match formula (percentage of your deferral, percentage of salary, cap on the match, cap
on eligible deferral), vesting on employer contributions, contribution limits, plan investment options (a
decent low-cost index lineup is a real benefit), and any discretionary contribution. The one-line
calculation: a 50% match up to 6% of salary means your employer adds 3% of salary; compounded over five
years that is real money — and a two-year cliff is worth knowing about.

**Leave.** Price it honestly. Annual leave: days granted × your daily rate. Public holidays observed in
your country, and how many the company actually gives. Sick leave — paid, unpaid, capped or unlimited-
and-untracked. Parental leave: weeks, all parents or primary only, fully paid, and whether tenure and
equity continue during it. Bereavement. Sabbatical policy if one exists — sabbaticals at senior levels are
real, quantifiable value worth asking about explicitly.

**Equity-adjacent value that is easy to miss.** Refresh grants (recurring value absent from a one-year
comparison, 15.3.4); off-cycle promotion grants; education and conference budgets including travel;
certification or exam cost coverage; equipment budgets and whether you choose the hardware; home-office
setup and whether it survives termination; commuter benefits. Then on-call compensation, relocation detail
(below), legal fees for contract review, immigration or visa support including dependents, severance terms,
and unused PTO payout.

**Work-model benefits.** Remote stipend and equipment, coworking allowance, travel frequency and
expectations, and — most important — how the written policy is enforced in practice. Ask current
employees; the written policy and the practice diverge nearly everywhere.

**How to negotiate benefits.** Rarely item by item. What works: "Is there flexibility in the sign-on to
offset what I'm losing on healthcare?" — the company cares far less about which form compensation takes than
you do. Ask for a one-time payment to bridge a coverage gap when changing plans. In a competitive market,
candidates who ask precise informed questions about benefits get taken more seriously; specificity is
itself a signal. Where a benefit is a real hardship — family coverage cost, a needed medical device, a
school-age child's needs — a case-specific accommodation is often possible, and HR is generally more
flexible than candidates assume.

**Who to ask.** The recruiter for plan documents and official written policies; benefits teams directly for
plan specifics (they will answer, and asking signals you read the paperwork); and your *future colleagues*
for reality. Both are necessary, and only the second predicts your experience. **The summary:** convert
every benefit you will actually use into annual dollars for the spreadsheet; treat the rest as zero.

keyConcepts: What to flag to a lawyer

interviewQuestions.text: "Could you send the employment agreement, IP assignment, and any

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Read before you sign.** The moment of signature is when your leverage is lowest. Read the employment
agreement, IP assignment, confidentiality agreement, any non-compete, and the equity plan documents
*before* accepting, and ask questions while you still have alternatives.

**Non-competes.** A restriction on working in the same industry, at the same companies, or in the same
role, for a period after you leave, often with compensation attached. Enforceability varies sharply by
jurisdiction: void or unenforceable in some places, strictly enforced and well-paid in others. Do not
assume — have a lawyer in the relevant jurisdiction tell you, or at minimum check the statutory position
for where you will live and where the company is incorporated.

**What to look for.** *Scope*: all industries, all companies above a size, or a named competitor list? A
clause barring any software work in a broad field is materially different from one naming competitors.
*Duration*: six months is very different from two years. *Geography*: nationwide is very different from one
metro area. *Compensation during the restriction*: paid restrictions are often enforceable and sometimes
valuable; unpaid ones are what get litigated. *Interaction with at-will*. *Choice of law and venue*, which
may not be your state. *Garden leave*: paid non-solicitation or non-dealing periods, sometimes at a
fraction of salary.

**Practical response.** Ask before accepting, neutrally: "I'd like to review the IP assignment and any
restrictive covenants — could you send them in advance so I'm not rushed?" Completely normal; a
reasonable recruiter will not blink. A company that requires you to sign something unreviewed at offer
stage is telling you how it will treat you later.

**Non-solicitation** is separate and common, usually narrower and more enforceable than a non-compete.
Understand it, because it constrains your next job's ability to recruit from them and may extend to
"employees" broadly — ask whether that means everyone at signing, everyone at termination, or your team.

**IP assignment.** Mostly reasonable by default. Check the *scope of "inventions"* — whether it covers
anything conceived during employment or everything touching the employer's business; a properly scoped
clause covers work product created with employer resources or relating to their business, while a clause
capturing independent work is a problem. Check for *prior-invention exclusions*: if there is no schedule
listing what you brought with you, ask to add one and attach a written list of your prior work. Note
*moral rights waivers* in some jurisdictions. Check *post-termination obligations* — how long, and
whether it purports to reach general skills and knowledge, which no agreement can legitimately extinguish.
And check how it *interacts with open source and side projects*: whether outside work is permitted and
whether anything is restricted.

**Confidentiality.** Understand the survival period, whether it purports to cover information you knew from
a *previous* employer — it cannot reasonably require you to keep your old employer's secrets from your new
one, though this arises in practice and is a real ethical situation — and whether anything is carved out
for general knowledge and skills. Include the right to discuss your work in general, non-confidential
terms, because a clause prohibiting even that is genuinely awkward in interviews.

**Equity plan documents.** Read the grant agreement, the plan, exercise and sale restrictions, the
post-termination exercise window, good/bad leaver provisions, and change-of-control treatment. Confirm your
grant is or will be reflected in a board-approved plan and that you will receive a copy. Confirm treatment
on termination for cause versus without cause.

**Other clauses to check.** At-will versus fixed term; offer contingencies that would void the offer
(background check, references, immigration status, signing-bonus clawback) and that you understand; the
notice period and whether resigning forfeits the signing bonus — almost always it does, so confirm the
clawback period and exceptions; bonus plan terms (discretionary or written criteria, and whether
clawback applies after payment); relocation repayment provisions; arbitration clauses and class-action
waivers, which mean giving up a jury and class actions; governing law and venue; death and disability
provisions for equity; and change-of-control treatment of unvested equity.

**What to flag to a lawyer.** Everything above if the package is material, plus any non-compete, unusual
IP language, anything unusual for your jurisdiction, anything you do not understand, and any change made to
a document after your first review. One hour with a lawyer in your jurisdiction is cheap insurance on a
package worth six figures a year.

**Questions to ask the recruiter.** "Could you send the employment agreement, IP assignment, and any
restrictive covenants in advance?" "Are there contingencies attached to the offer?" "Is there a clawback
on the signing bonus, and over what period?" "Will I get the equity plan documents before I sign?" "Is
there anything specific to this role or this jurisdiction?" None of these are unreasonable, and all are
better asked before you accept.

topics.description: Relocation terms within Offer and Negotiation.
keyConcepts: Know what "relocation" includes, because packages vary enormously
The clawback is the term that matters most
When relocation is not worth it

interviewQuestions.text: Total value of the package and which parts are taxable? Is there a gross-up? What

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Know what "relocation" includes, because packages vary enormously.** Temporary housing (weeks or
months, what standard, taxable?); a lump sum or reimbursed expenses, and whether it is taxable;
house-hunting trips and who pays travel; household-goods shipment with coverage limits; loss-on-sale
coverage on your current home; commuter or interim living assistance if your household cannot move
immediately; family support — partner job search help, school placement, dependent visas; mortgage
assistance or buyout of a remaining lease; visits back to your origin city; and the eligibility timeline
plus what happens if you leave within 6, 12, or 24 months.

**The clawback is the term that matters most.** Most packages require staying for a period, typically one
year, sometimes two. Leaving early can trigger repayment of the full or a prorated amount. Ask for exact
written terms, and ask whether the clause survives if you are terminated, if the role changes, or if a
spouse's career is the reason you cannot follow. Getting the carve-outs in writing is worth real money,
because the most common reason to leave early is a family or health event you could not have predicted.

**Tax treatment.** Relocation benefits are generally taxable unless you meet a statutory exclusion for
employees meeting distance or time requirements in many jurisdictions. Ask whether the package is
grossed up — the company paying tax on your behalf — which is a material difference in net value. Compute
the after-tax amount; a taxable package is worth noticeably less than its face.

**House-hunting discipline.** Do not buy a house before your start date. New hires make expensive
decisions under interstate-move pressure. Rent for the first several months, visit neighborhoods in
person, and use the temporary housing period as the exploration window. This is the single most common
early mistake in relocation and very hard to undo.

**Cost it yourself, comprehensively.** Beyond the package: your housing-cost delta; moving costs; dual
housing; school or childcare changes; commute time in the new city; visits home for the family; and often
largest, the effect on a partner's career and social network. A package offsetting three months of dual
housing is not compensation for a trailing partner's career cost, even though many people treat it as if
it were.

**Remote-in-hybrid reality.** If the role is hybrid in the new city, verify before signing: how many
days, per-team or per-company, can it change after you start, and is the office where the work is or a
formality. Then check the office location. A "hybrid" role in a suburb with bad transit is a hidden
relocation failure.

**Questions to ask.** Total value of the package and which parts are taxable? Is there a gross-up? What
is the minimum stay and the clawback formula, and what are the carve-outs? What is temporary housing
like — where, how long, what size? Can I get a home-finding visit, and when should I arrive? What does
the team do about hybrid schedules in practice? What help exists for a partner's job search and dependent
visas?

**Negotiation points.** People routinely negotiate a longer temporary housing period, a non-clawed
portion, a larger lump sum, coverage for a partner's job search, or flexibility to start remotely for the
first month and relocate later. These are often easier to get than base money, because they come from a
different budget.

**When relocation is not worth it.** If the destination's cost of living is dramatically higher, the
package will not close the gap and the headline number is misleading. Do the arithmetic on net cash in
hand, not on the offer letter. And if a partner's career is sacrificed, decide explicitly whether that is
acceptable rather than discovering later.

largest, the effect on a partner's career and social network. A package offsetting three months of dual

it were.

days, per-team or per-company, can it change after you start, and is the office where the work is or a
formality. Then check the office location. A "hybrid" role in a suburb with bad transit is a hidden
relocation failure.

is the minimum stay and the clawback formula, and what are the carve-outs? What is temporary housing
like — where, how long, what size? Can I get a home-finding visit, and when should I arrive? What does
the team do about hybrid schedules in practice? What help exists for a partner's job search and dependent
visas?

**Negotiation points.** People routinely negotiate a longer temporary housing period, a non-clawed
portion, a larger lump sum, coverage for a partner's job search, or flexibility to start remotely for the
first month and relocate later. These are often easier to get than base money, because they come from a
different budget.

**When relocation is not worth it.** If the destination's cost of living is dramatically higher, the
package will not close the gap and the headline number is misleading. Do the arithmetic on net cash in
hand, not on the offer letter. And if a partner's career is sacrificed, decide explicitly whether that is
acceptable rather than discovering later.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**The work model as compensation.** Remote, hybrid, and onsite are different jobs with different totals.
Adjust: commute time has a real annual cost in hours, and those hours are not recoverable. A fully remote
offer in a lower-cost city can net more than a higher base onsite elsewhere. Model after-tax and
after-commute.

**Questions to settle before signing.** Required office days per week, and whether it is a company policy,
team policy, or one manager's preference — get the answer from two people, because these diverge. Who
chooses which days, and are core days imposed. What "remote" means geographically: same time zone, same
country, anywhere; same country usually implies local employment terms, which is safer for you.
Compensation by location, whether the offer is location-specific, and what happens if you later move.
Time-zone overlap hours and whether meetings are distributed or concentrated. Travel frequency and who
pays. Equipment and connectivity budgets and whether they survive termination. And what happens to your
role if the policy changes later — realistically they can change it, so know how much notice you would get.

**Red flags in remote arrangements.** "Remote" with more on-site days than the local team gets; a policy
changeable at any time without notice; location-specific pay that would cut substantially if you relocate;
no written statement of your employment country and governing law; unstated material travel expectations;
and being remote in a country where the company has no entity, which creates an employment-classification
and tax problem you inherit.

**Employer of record for international remote.** If you are not in a country where the company has an
entity, you may be engaged as a contractor or through an employer of record. The consequences are real:
employment protections, benefits, paid leave, notice periods, and tax treatment may all be weaker or
absent, and your employment status may be less secure. Ask directly which entity employs you and in which
jurisdiction. A vague answer is important information.

**Visa and sponsorship — assess honestly.** *Type*: employment visas typically require employer
sponsorship and tie you to a specific role and employer; intra-company transfers differ and are often
better; independent work permits are strongest and hardest. *Track record*: how many people have been
sponsored successfully in the last two years — ask for a number. *Timing*: processes run from weeks to
many months; get the timeline in writing including your part and theirs, and know who pays for filings and
government fees. *Dependents*: whether family can accompany you and the mechanism. *Duration and
constraints*: permanent or temporary, whether tied to your role (moving roles internally may require a new
filing), and how long you have to leave if employment ends. *Long-term path*: green card or permanent
residency support, at what stage, and any legal-fee benefit. *Costs*: filing fees, legal fees,
translations, reimbursable or not. And *restrictions on your own activities*, since many visas limit
self-employment or outside work — read the terms.

**Sponsorship red flags.** Being asked to buy your own sponsorship — legitimate visa services exist, but a
company pressuring you to pay for a visa it is obliged to sponsor is a bad sign. "We will sponsor after
you prove yourself" — companies rarely retroactively sponsor. No timeline, no named process, no lawyer
contact. An offer contingent on visa approval with no stated remedy if denied: ask what happens to your
offer and your status if the visa is refused. Your status depending on a single employer in a weak market
for that employer.

**The correct sequence.** Have a specialist immigration lawyer review before you resign from anything.
Understand whether the company has a documented process, your timeline, and your fallback. Do not resign
until the process has a clear start date with the company — a filed application with a receipt is
meaningfully better than a promise.

**Equity with visa status.** Stock for non-citizens carries tax and reporting complications, including
forms and obligations that vary by status. Ask the equity administrator what they support and what
reporting you own, and get tax advice specific to your status. Also ask whether equity is granted at all
in your jurisdiction.

**The non-negotiable question.** "If the visa is delayed or denied, what is the status of my offer and
what are my options?" If they cannot answer, you have a hope, not a plan.

🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**

**Resignation mechanics.** Check your contract for the required notice period and whether it must be in
writing. Deliver notice in person or by email to your manager and HR, with a short professional letter
giving your last working day and thanks. Brief, positive, free of reasons. Reasons belong in a separate
private conversation if at all — never in the written resignation, and never as an announcement to
colleagues.

**The notice period.** Give what you are contractually required to give. Giving less to start faster is a
small gain for a real cost: the goodwill that produces your references, your alumni network, and future
help. If you have an urgent reason — health, family, safety — ask your manager and HR privately for a
shortened notice; it is granted more often than candidates expect, and far more often when asked directly
than when handled by simply not showing up.

**Do not burn bridges, in the specific ways that matter.** Do not trash the company, team, or manager to
anyone; assume your words reach them, and they often do. Do not take or forward anything proprietary — code,
documents, data, contacts. Do not use your last weeks to recruit your own team to your next employer: it is
a hostile act even when the company is not staying, and it is widely punished. Do leave working code in
good shape — finish or hand off your work, update documentation, write the runbook for whoever inherits
it. This is the strongest predictor of a good reference. Return all property — laptop, badge, keys,
credentials, cards — and get written confirmation. Complete exit paperwork and knowledge transfer, and keep
copies of what you sign.

**The handover is the reference.** Write a document listing what you owned, where it is, how it works,
what is fragile, and what is in flight, then give an oral walkthrough. People remember the colleague who
made their transition easy.

**The exit conversation.** Ask for feedback on your performance while you still have leverage to act on
it, and write it down. Ask about the reference process and who will be contacted, and correct factual
errors now — a wrong title or project description in a reference is expensive and much easier to fix now.

**Keep the relationships you want to keep.** Your manager, closest colleagues, and mentor are who will
speak for you in two years. Tell them the news yourself before it is announced, tell them the real reason
in confidence, and ask directly — "Will you write me a reference if I need one in a year?" Answers given
in advance are reliable; answers extracted later are not.

**The alumni network as a durable asset.** Keep the internal Slack channels, group chats, mailing lists,
and community accounts (community Slack usually keeps you after you leave). Stay in touch deliberately —
occasional messages, things they would find useful, congratulations. Go back and visit or speak to your
old team when invited; it costs an hour and keeps you in the group's memory. Offer help to your former
teammates when you can: that is what keeps a network warm and what people remember when they need a
referral. Do not use your old team for information about your new employer's confidential matters, and do
not bring your old employer's confidential information anywhere. The reverse also holds: your network does
not disappear when you leave, and most referrals and hiring information come from the outside.

**Non-compete and non-solicitation, once more.** Know exactly what you can and cannot do in your first
ninety days, and get legal advice if the clause is broad or your next role is adjacent. Do not bring your
old company's code, documents, or confidential information to your new job. If in doubt about whether
something is confidential, ask your lawyer, not your new employer.

**First-day preparation.** Confirm start date, equipment shipment, badge, accounts, and first-week
schedule. Bring the contacts you need. Re-read the team documentation. Do not start a big project in week
one; start conversations.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Why the first quarter determines the outcome.** Almost all engineers who fail at a new job fail in the
first quarter, and almost always for the same four predictable reasons: they did not learn the system fast
enough, did not build relationships, did not deliver anything visible, or were too quiet to find out what
mattered. A plan written now prevents all four.

**Days 1–30: listen and map.**
- *Systems map*: the main services, data stores, deploy pipeline, alerting, on-call rotation — written
  down. Read the docs and code; ask the most senior person on the team for a tour.
- *People map*: immediate collaborators, manager's peers, cross-team dependencies, skip-level. For each,
  learn what they own and what they need from you. Thirty-day informal conversations are cheap and define
  the next two quarters.
- *Understand success*: get your manager's explicit definition of 30/60/90-day and 12-month success, in
  writing if possible, then repeat it back and confirm.
- *Ship something small but real* — a bug fix, a small feature, a test, a documented fix. The purpose is
  completing the entire loop: understand, change, deploy, observe. You are learning the system, not
  contributing significant code.
- *Ask about constraints*: what is off-limits, what broke last time, what the team wishes it had done
  differently.
- *Set up your environment in week one*: every system, the alerting you own, the dashboards you need,
  deploy rights.

**Days 31–60: contribute and diagnose.**
- *Own a deliverable* with a 6–8 week scope you can complete. Not huge — a project that ships and
  demonstrates competence.
- *Diagnose something*: fix a recurring problem, reduce an alert, close a ticket category, improve a flaky
  area. Diagnosis is high-visibility, low-risk, and teaches the system's real state.
- *Ask for feedback around day 45* — mid-point, not year-end: "What should I keep doing, and what should
  I stop doing?"
- *Fill the gaps you found*: return to the systems and people maps and close the holes. Teams with no such
  map are why new hires are useless for months.
- *Join the team's rituals*: code review, design review, incident review. Learn the review norms by
  reviewing early and often.
- *One visible improvement with a metric*: a small metric reduction, a documented process, a documented
  migration path, a test suite that removes a class of bug.

**Days 61–90: own a domain and start compounding.**
- *Take ownership of a system or subsystem* with clear boundaries, and write down what you own.
- *Propose a larger change* — migration, redesign, performance project — in writing, naming the problem,
  options, risks, and phasing. Do not implement it unilaterally; write it and let the team react.
- *Extend your network* to adjacent teams and the wider organization; present at an internal tech talk or
  write an internal doc where the culture allows it.
- *Have the longer-term conversation* with your manager: level expectations, promotion timeline, what you
  want to be doing in a year, what you need from them.
- *Build on-call readiness*: shadow a shift before you are on it.
- *Give back*: mentor, review, fix something outside your immediate area.

**The 30/60/90 conversation with your manager.** Propose it yourself in week one. Most managers welcome it
because it removes ambiguity, and it is a strong seniority signal. Keep it as a living document updated
in your one-on-ones.

**What to avoid in the first 90 days.** Do not redesign anything before you understand why it is that way.
Do not lead with opinions about the stack in month one — listen first, you will be told the constraints. Do
not become the loudest voice in the room; volume early reads as inexperience. Do not fix things nobody
asked you to fix, however tempting — symptom fixes without understanding cause damage relationships. Do not
skip the boring parts: the deploy pipeline, the on-call rotation, the incident history; skipping them is
why new hires cannot be given real work. Do not vanish into your ticket queue; visible small wins beat
invisible throughput. Do not complain about your previous employer, even obliquely.

**Making the plan real.** Before your start date, write down the systems and people to map, the
deliverable, the diagnosis, the proposal, and the 30/60/90 checkpoints with dates. Bring it to week one
and reconcile it with your manager. People who arrive with a written plan get treated as owners from week
one, because they behave like owners from week one. A fill-in template is in the templates section.
